name: Jayma Abdoo
description: Youngest documented member of the Camden 28, age 20 at the 1971 indictment. Graduate of Immaculate Heart Academy, Bergen County NJ; her antiwar involvement began with the 1968 McCarthy campaign. Worked as a children's librarian. Acquitted with all defendants in the 1973 jury-nullification trial.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: William Anderson
description: Westmont, NJ osteopathic physician, age 36 at indictment, father of six. His practice served Camden's poor Puerto Rican community and elderly residents of the McGuire Housing Project. Graduate of Temple University College of Pharmacy and the Philadelphia College of Osteopathic Medicine. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Milo Billman
description: Lutheran minister, age 39 at indictment, ordained 1958. The only Protestant clergyman among the Camden 28. Worked with Appalachians near Cincinnati, helped develop Columbus (Ohio) ECCO anti-poverty foundation, and was Outreach Director of Camden's EPOC. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Terry Buckalew
description: Age 21 at indictment; valedictorian of Wildwood Catholic High School, NJ, and recipient of a John F. Kennedy award for courage and moral integrity. Attended Rider College and worked as a court clerk in the Federal Third Circuit of Appeals. Had refused induction into the armed forces. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Paul Couming
description: Age 23 at indictment; Boston Technical School graduate and former VISTA volunteer in Appalachia. A member of the 'Boston 8', sentenced (suspended) for refusing to carry his draft cards, and charged with criminal contempt for refusing to answer the Harrisburg Grand Jury. Acquitted with the Camden 28 in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Eugene Dixon
description: Camden resident and father of four, age 37 at indictment, employed 20 years as a supervisor for a Philadelphia automotive firm. A prize-winning poet active as an officer/teacher in the Confraternity of Christian Doctrine and in the PTA. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Anne Dunham
description: Age 23 at indictment; native of Pelham, NY, graduate of Ursuline Academy who attended Marymount College and the College of New Rochelle. Taught Confraternity of Christian Doctrine, tutored in Harlem, and worked for the Archdiocese of NY Board of Education and Resistance Book Distributors. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Peter Fordi
description: Jesuit priest, age 35 at indictment, based at Woodstock Religious College, NYC; native of Jersey City who entered the Society of Jesus in 1956. Had already taken public responsibility (with the East Coast Conspiracy to Save Lives) for the February 1970 Philadelphia draft-board and Washington GE-office raids. At trial he declared 'I ripped up those files with my hands.' Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Keith Forsyth
description: Age 22 at indictment; Ohio native who moved to Philadelphia and worked as a cab driver, active with the October 4th Organization in Kensington. Acquitted with the Camden 28 in 1973. In 2014 he publicly revealed he had been one of the burglars of the March 1971 FBI office break-in in Media, PA that exposed COINTELPRO.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Michael Giocondo
description: Former Franciscan brother (12 years, stationed in Costa Rica and Washington DC), age 42 at indictment. Worked in Camden where he founded El Centro, an inner-city service for Spanish speakers, and co-founded the bilingual newspaper GAP. It was Giocondo who first brought Bob Hardy into the group. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Robert Good
description: Age 22 at indictment; a former seminarian who studied five years with the Missionary Society of the Divine Word and attended Xavier University, Cincinnati. Active in the Cleveland civil-rights movement; at the time a NYC resident working with the Harrisburg Defense Committee. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Margaret Innes
description: Boston native, age 27 at indictment; held a BA from Regis College and was completing an MA at Boston College in special education. A former novice of the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur, she taught in Dorchester public schools. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Edward McGowan
description: Jesuit (13 years), age 36 at indictment, resident of Woodstock College and a Bronx native considered an expert on American Indian affairs. Worked with Fr. Philip Berrigan in a Baltimore ghetto parish, participated in draft-board raids with the New York 8, and was active with the Harrisburg Defense Committee. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Francis Mel Madden
description: Boston native, age 33 at indictment; ordained a Franciscan priest in 1965. Founded Liberty Village, a drug-treatment center in Jersey City (1967), and was later married with two children. Former director of training for NJ's Drug Education Program, suspended without pay at his arrest. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Lianne Moccia
description: Native of Revere, Massachusetts, age 21 at indictment; a part-time senior at Fordham University who graduated from Mt. St. Joseph's Academy, Brighton. Worked with the Christian Appalachian Project and at the Bronx Resistance Book Store and Defense Committee. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Barry Musi
description: Massachusetts native, age 23 at indictment; a draft and military counselor who left his conscientious-objector alternate service in January 1971 and moved to Dorchester for community and movement work. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Edward Murphy
description: Jesuit priest and NYC native, age 34 at indictment; entered the Society of Jesus in 1955, ordained 1968, taught Classics and Theology. A member of the New York 8, he ran a GI coffeehouse near Fort Devens, MA, worked as a draft counselor, and was a national coordinator of the Harrisburg Defense Committee. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Frank Pommersheim
description: New York native, age 28 at indictment; Colgate University graduate and Columbia Law School alumnus who had been a VISTA lawyer in Alaska. Acquitted with the Camden 28 in 1973. Went on to a distinguished career as a professor of law at the University of South Dakota and a leading scholar/jurist of federal Indian law.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Joan Reilly
description: Age 20 at indictment; from Brightwaters, Long Island, a psychology/philosophy junior at Marymount College, Tarrytown, and elected student senator. Volunteered with the Christian Appalachian Project. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Rosemary Reilly
description: Age 22 at indictment; from Brightwaters, Long Island, graduate of the Academy of Saint Joseph who attended Newton College of the Sacred Heart and Marymount-Manhattan. Managed the Resistance Book Distributors office in New York and worked with the NY Defense Committee. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Anita Ricci
description: Philadelphia native, age 22 at indictment; graduated fifth in her class at St. Maria Goretti High School, won a scholarship to the University of Pennsylvania and studied sociology at Temple. Worked at the Resistance Book Store in Philadelphia. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Kathleen Ridolfi
description: South Philadelphia native ('Cookie'), age 23 at indictment; attended Temple University and Philadelphia Textile College and managed the Resistance Book Store on Temple's campus. Also named in the Harrisburg case indictment. Acquitted with the Camden 28 in 1973. Later a law professor and founder of the Northern California Innocence Project at Santa Clara University.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Martha Shemeley
description: Camden social worker, age 34 at indictment and mother of a ten-year-old; formerly taught in the Camden diocese. A Seton Hall psychology graduate and published Catholic-press writer who lectured on 'The Underground Church' and the role of women in the church. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: John Swinglish
description: From Cleveland, Ohio, living in Washington DC, age 28 at indictment; a Navy veteran who did Defense Department research on nuclear guided-missile destroyers and formerly chaired the Catholic Peace Fellowship in DC. Indicted for criminal contempt after refusing to testify to the Harrisburg grand jury and named a co-conspirator there. Acquitted with the Camden 28 in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Sarah Tosi
description: From Ho-Ho-Kus, NJ, age 20 at indictment; a 1969 Immaculate Heart Academy graduate and National Honor Society president, NJ district coordinator for the 1968 McCarthy campaign. Attended Wellesley College, was active in Boston's Paulist Center, and did community work in Dorchester. Acquitted in 1973.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: Robert Williamson
description: Age 22 at indictment; employed as a caseworker for the Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare. Acquitted with the Camden 28 in 1973. In 2014 he was one of the activists who publicly revealed his role in the March 1971 Media, PA FBI-office burglary that exposed COINTELPRO.

case.charges: Conspiracy and destruction of Selective Service records (the August 22, 1971 Camden, NJ draft-board raid).
case.convicted: No — acquitted by a jury in the 1973 trial.

name: John Michael Donner
description: Lead-named defendant in United States v. Donner, the federal case against the Beaver 55 for destroying 1-A and delinquent draft files in 44 local boards at the Indianapolis Selective Service headquarters on Oct 31, 1969. Convicted on all four counts (one count later reversed on appeal); originally sentenced to four years, reduced to three. By 1974 he had joined the Divine Light Mission and become its National Executive Director.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the October 31, 1969 Indianapolis raid) — United States v. Donner.
case.convicted: Convicted; two of the eight received probation.

name: Jane Anne Kennedy
description: A nurse and nursing educator with a master's degree, the oldest Beaver 55 member. She took part in scrambling magnetic research tapes at Dow Chemical (Midland, Michigan) and, a week later, destroying draft files in Indianapolis. Convicted on all four counts in the Indianapolis case (four years, reduced to three) and served a separate Michigan sentence for the Dow action; the opinion notes she expressed no remorse. She was released from the federal women's prison at Alderson, West Virginia in the mid-1970s.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the October 31, 1969 Indianapolis raid) — United States v. Donner.
case.convicted: Convicted; two of the eight received probation.

name: Paul Joseph Mack
description: The youngest Beaver 55 defendant, age 18 at the time of the Indianapolis draft-board raid. Convicted on all four counts and sentenced to four years plus a $5,000 fine (later reduced by a year); his case was reversed and remanded for resentencing over a Youth Corrections Act violation.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the October 31, 1969 Indianapolis raid) — United States v. Donner.
case.convicted: Convicted; two of the eight received probation.

name: Connie Grubbs McNamara
description: One of the eight Beaver 55 defendants prosecuted for the Oct 31, 1969 destruction of draft files at the Indianapolis Selective Service headquarters. Named (as Connie Grubbs McNamara) among the group that publicly claimed responsibility at press conferences in Washington and Indianapolis in November 1969. Specific individual sentence not separately identified in available sources; the opinion notes two of the eight received probation.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the October 31, 1969 Indianapolis raid) — United States v. Donner.
case.convicted: Convicted; two of the eight received probation.

name: Marty McNamara
description: One of the eight Beaver 55 defendants in the Indianapolis draft-file destruction case (United States v. Donner). Named among the members who claimed responsibility for erasing/destroying files at 44 Indianapolis draft boards on Oct 31, 1969. Individual sentence not separately identified in available sources.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the October 31, 1969 Indianapolis raid) — United States v. Donner.
case.convicted: Convicted; two of the eight received probation.

name: Jo Ann Mulert
description: One of the eight Beaver 55 defendants prosecuted for the Oct 31, 1969 raid on the Indianapolis Selective Service headquarters. Named in the group's public claim of responsibility. Individual sentence not separately identified in available sources.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the October 31, 1969 Indianapolis raid) — United States v. Donner.
case.convicted: Convicted; two of the eight received probation.

name: Thomas Trost
description: One of the eight Beaver 55 members; credited with coining the group's whimsical name (the group was only eight people, not 55). A participant in the Indianapolis draft-file destruction of Oct 31, 1969 and prosecuted in United States v. Donner. Individual sentence not separately identified in available sources.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the October 31, 1969 Indianapolis raid) — United States v. Donner.
case.convicted: Convicted; two of the eight received probation.

name: David Williams
description: One of the eight Beaver 55 defendants prosecuted for the destruction of draft files at 44 Indianapolis draft boards on Oct 31, 1969. Named among the members who publicly claimed responsibility in November 1969. Individual sentence not separately identified in available sources.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the October 31, 1969 Indianapolis raid) — United States v. Donner.
case.convicted: Convicted; two of the eight received probation.

name: Chuck Turchick
description: Member of the Alexandria raiding team (with Bill Tilton and Cliff Ulen) arrested during the July 10, 1970 Minnesota Eight actions against Selective Service offices. Convicted Nov 5, 1970 and sentenced to five years in federal prison; served roughly 14-20 months and was released in July 1973. Known for calling Judge Edward Devitt 'a pompous ass' at a co-defendant's trial, drawing a 10-day contempt term.

case.charges: Interfering with the Selective Service System (the July 1970 Minnesota draft-board raids).
case.convicted: Convicted; most sentenced to five years and released July 1973.

name: Bill Tilton
description: Member of the Alexandria raiding team arrested in the July 10, 1970 Minnesota Eight actions. Convicted Nov 5, 1970 and sentenced to five years in federal prison; released July 1973. At sentencing he told Judge Devitt he was 'a good German' enabling fascism. He later became a St. Paul attorney.

case.charges: Interfering with the Selective Service System (the July 1970 Minnesota draft-board raids).
case.convicted: Convicted; most sentenced to five years and released July 1973.

name: Cliff Ulen
description: Member of the Alexandria raiding team in the July 10, 1970 Minnesota Eight actions. The only one of the eight to plead guilty; he received no prison time.

case.charges: Interfering with the Selective Service System (the July 1970 Minnesota draft-board raids).
case.convicted: Convicted; most sentenced to five years and released July 1973.

name: Don Olson
description: Member of the Winona raiding team (with Peter Simmons and Brad Beneke) arrested in the July 10, 1970 Minnesota Eight actions. Convicted Dec 3, 1970 and sentenced to five years in federal prison; released July 1973. Remained a longtime Twin Cities peace and community-radio activist.

case.charges: Interfering with the Selective Service System (the July 1970 Minnesota draft-board raids).
case.convicted: Convicted; most sentenced to five years and released July 1973.

name: Peter Simmons
description: Member of the Winona raiding team in the July 10, 1970 Minnesota Eight actions. Convicted Dec 3, 1970; because he was among the two youngest defendants he received an indeterminate sentence under youthful-offender status rather than the flat five years.

case.charges: Interfering with the Selective Service System (the July 1970 Minnesota draft-board raids).
case.convicted: Convicted; most sentenced to five years and released July 1973.

name: Brad Beneke
description: Member of the Winona raiding team in the July 10, 1970 Minnesota Eight actions. Convicted Dec 3, 1970; as one of the two youngest defendants he received an indeterminate sentence under youthful-offender status.

case.charges: Interfering with the Selective Service System (the July 1970 Minnesota draft-board raids).
case.convicted: Convicted; most sentenced to five years and released July 1973.

name: Francis Kroncke
description: Member of the Little Falls raiding team (with Michael Therriault) in the July 10, 1970 Minnesota Eight actions. Convicted Jan 18, 1971 and sentenced to five years in federal prison; released July 1973. A former Catholic seminarian/theology teacher, he later compiled and preserved archival materials documenting the Minnesota Eight trials.

case.charges: Interfering with the Selective Service System (the July 1970 Minnesota draft-board raids).
case.convicted: Convicted; most sentenced to five years and released July 1973.

name: Michael Therriault
description: Member of the Little Falls raiding team in the July 10, 1970 Minnesota Eight actions. Convicted Jan 18, 1971 and sentenced to five years in federal prison; released July 1973.

case.charges: Interfering with the Selective Service System (the July 1970 Minnesota draft-board raids).
case.convicted: Convicted; most sentenced to five years and released July 1973.

name: Joseph T. Gilchrist
description: Known as Joe Gilchrist, a former Cornell student (there during Fr. Daniel Berrigan's chaplaincy) from Ithaca, NY, and one of the eight arrested Sept 6, 1970 in the Rochester raids. He was the only defendant represented by legal counsel and planned to appeal. Convicted and sentenced to two to three years.

case.charges: Raiding and destroying records at Rochester's Selective Service, FBI, and U.S. Attorney offices (September 6, 1970).
case.convicted: Convicted; sentenced to terms ranging from about 17 to 30 months.

name: Francis B. Callahan
description: Known as Frank Callahan, from Philadelphia, one of the eight Flower City Conspiracy members arrested Sept 6, 1970 for the Rochester draft-board/FBI-office raid. Convicted on all counts and sentenced to seventeen to twenty-two months.

case.charges: Raiding and destroying records at Rochester's Selective Service, FBI, and U.S. Attorney offices (September 6, 1970).
case.convicted: Convicted; sentenced to terms ranging from about 17 to 30 months.

name: Suzanne Williams
description: Known as Suzi Williams, of Rochester, NY, one of the eight arrested Sept 6, 1970. She conducted her own defense, cross-examining an FBI agent at trial. Convicted and sentenced to twenty to thirty months.

case.charges: Raiding and destroying records at Rochester's Selective Service, FBI, and U.S. Attorney offices (September 6, 1970).
case.convicted: Convicted; sentenced to terms ranging from about 17 to 30 months.

name: DeCourcy Squire
description: A Quaker antiwar activist and former Antioch College student from Cincinnati, known for a lengthy jail hunger strike (Dec 1967-Jan 1968) after an earlier arrest. One of the eight arrested Sept 6, 1970 in the Rochester raids; convicted and sentenced to twenty to thirty months by Judge Harold Burke. She later became a physical therapist and a lifelong war-tax resister and anti-hunger organizer (Just Harvest).

case.charges: Raiding and destroying records at Rochester's Selective Service, FBI, and U.S. Attorney offices (September 6, 1970).
case.convicted: Convicted; sentenced to terms ranging from about 17 to 30 months.

name: Jane Meyerding
description: One of the eight Flower City Conspiracy members arrested Sept 6, 1970 for the Rochester draft-board and FBI-office raid. Convicted on all counts and sentenced to seventeen to twenty-two months. Later known as a writer.

case.charges: Raiding and destroying records at Rochester's Selective Service, FBI, and U.S. Attorney offices (September 6, 1970).
case.convicted: Convicted; sentenced to terms ranging from about 17 to 30 months.

name: Joan Nicholson
description: At 36 the oldest of the eight Flower City Conspiracy defendants, from Philadelphia. Arrested Sept 6, 1970 in the Rochester raids; convicted and sentenced to twenty to thirty months.

case.charges: Raiding and destroying records at Rochester's Selective Service, FBI, and U.S. Attorney offices (September 6, 1970).
case.convicted: Convicted; sentenced to terms ranging from about 17 to 30 months.

name: Wayne Bonekemper
description: A Rochester, NY resident and one of the eight arrested Sept 6, 1970 for the draft-board and FBI-office raid. Convicted on all counts and sentenced to twenty to thirty months.

case.charges: Raiding and destroying records at Rochester's Selective Service, FBI, and U.S. Attorney offices (September 6, 1970).
case.convicted: Convicted; sentenced to terms ranging from about 17 to 30 months.

name: Robert T. Begin
description: A Roman Catholic diocesan priest of the Diocese of Cleveland, Begin was one of the nine (mostly Catholic clergy and religious) who on March 22, 1969 raided the Dow Chemical Company offices in Washington, D.C., smashing glass, throwing files out a fourth-floor window and pouring blood on records to protest Dow's manufacture of napalm and nerve gas. He was charged with malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry. He was sentenced (terms across the group ranged from a few months to several years) but, like most of the group, did not ultimately serve time after appeals overturned convictions in 1972.

case.charges: Malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry (the March 22, 1969 raid on Dow Chemical's Washington, DC offices).
case.convicted: Convicted; most convictions reversed on appeal in 1972.

name: Michael R. Dougherty
description: A former Roman Catholic priest and former U.S. Army paratrooper, Dougherty was one of the nine who raided the Dow Chemical offices in Washington, D.C. on March 22, 1969, destroying files and pouring blood to protest napalm production. He was charged with malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry and sentenced along with the others. Convictions for most of the group (including seven who appealed) were reversed in 1972.

case.charges: Malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry (the March 22, 1969 raid on Dow Chemical's Washington, DC offices).
case.convicted: Convicted; most convictions reversed on appeal in 1972.

name: Joann Malone
description: A Roman Catholic nun and member of the Sisters of Loretto (a schoolteacher, formerly teaching in Montgomery, Alabama and St. Louis), Malone joined the DC Nine raid on Dow Chemical on March 22, 1969. She is noted as the first nun in U.S. history to commit five federal felonies and be convicted, facing a potential 35 years; the reaction at her Catholic school in St. Louis caused it to close for a week. She went on to a lifelong career as a labor organizer and public high-school social studies teacher in the DC/Maryland area; convictions were reversed on appeal in 1972.

case.charges: Malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry (the March 22, 1969 raid on Dow Chemical's Washington, DC offices).
case.convicted: Convicted; most convictions reversed on appeal in 1972.

name: Arthur G. Melville
description: A former Maryknoll priest who, with his brother Thomas Melville, had been a missionary among the Maya in Guatemala until the Guatemalan government expelled them in December 1967 for their radical social-justice activism. Arthur left the priesthood and married former nun Catherine Melville; both were among the nine who raided the Dow Chemical offices on March 22, 1969. He was charged with malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry; convictions were reversed on appeal in 1972. (His brother Thomas and sister-in-law Marjorie Bradford Melville were members of the earlier Catonsville Nine.)

case.charges: Malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry (the March 22, 1969 raid on Dow Chemical's Washington, DC offices).
case.convicted: Convicted; most convictions reversed on appeal in 1972.

name: Catherine Melville
description: A former Roman Catholic nun and wife of former Maryknoll priest Arthur Melville, Catherine was one of the nine who raided the Dow Chemical offices in Washington, D.C. on March 22, 1969. She was charged with malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry. Notably, she was one of only two of the nine (with Rev. Bernard Meyer) who actually served jail time before the group's convictions were largely overturned on appeal in 1972.

case.charges: Malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry (the March 22, 1969 raid on Dow Chemical's Washington, DC offices).
case.convicted: Convicted; most convictions reversed on appeal in 1972.

name: Bernard Meyer
description: A Roman Catholic priest (associated with Cleveland, Ohio), Rev. Bernard Meyer was one of the nine who raided the Dow Chemical offices on March 22, 1969. He was charged with malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry. He was one of only two of the group (with Catherine Melville) who actually served time in jail.

case.charges: Malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry (the March 22, 1969 raid on Dow Chemical's Washington, DC offices).
case.convicted: Convicted; most convictions reversed on appeal in 1972.

name: Dennis J. Moloney
description: A Roman Catholic priest associated with Detroit, Michigan, Rev. Dennis Moloney was one of the nine who raided the Dow Chemical offices on March 22, 1969, destroying files and pouring blood over records to protest napalm and nerve-gas production. He was charged with malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry and sentenced with the group; most convictions were reversed on appeal in 1972.

case.charges: Malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry (the March 22, 1969 raid on Dow Chemical's Washington, DC offices).
case.convicted: Convicted; most convictions reversed on appeal in 1972.

name: Joseph F. O'Rourke
description: A Jesuit (Society of Jesus) then in formation (ordained a priest around 1971), O'Rourke joined the Jesuits in 1958 and was one of the nine who raided the Dow Chemical offices on March 22, 1969. He was charged with malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry. He later became nationally known when the Jesuits dismissed him in 1974 after he publicly baptized the child of a couple in an abortion-rights controversy; he remained a lifelong activist.

case.charges: Malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry (the March 22, 1969 raid on Dow Chemical's Washington, DC offices).
case.convicted: Convicted; most convictions reversed on appeal in 1972.

name: Michael Slaski
description: A young Catholic layperson from Detroit, Michigan, Slaski (age 20, the youngest of the group) was one of the nine who raided the Dow Chemical offices on March 22, 1969. He was charged with malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry and sentenced with the group; convictions were largely reversed on appeal in 1972.

case.charges: Malicious destruction of property and unlawful entry (the March 22, 1969 raid on Dow Chemical's Washington, DC offices).
case.convicted: Convicted; most convictions reversed on appeal in 1972.

name: Joseph E. Mulligan
description: A Jesuit seminarian (Society of Jesus) at the time, age 25, Mulligan was one of the fifteen who on May 25, 1969 broke into the Selective Service office at 2355 W. 63rd Street in Chicago, removed roughly 40,000 draft records and burned them in an alley, waiting to be arrested. He was among those convicted (10 of 11 tried were convicted in June 1970) and served prison time (group terms ran up to two years). Ordained a Jesuit priest in 1973, he spent decades as a liberation-theology missionary with Christian base communities in Nicaragua and wrote on the Jesuit martyrs of El Salvador.

case.charges: Destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy (the May 25, 1969 Chicago draft-record burning).
case.convicted: Most were convicted in June 1970.

name: John Pietra
description: A Roman Catholic priest (Fr. John Pietra, age 33), he was one of the fifteen who burned some 40,000 Chicago draft records on May 25, 1969. He was indicted on four federal counts (destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy) and was among those convicted in June 1970, with sentences running up to two years.

case.charges: Destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy (the May 25, 1969 Chicago draft-record burning).
case.convicted: Most were convicted in June 1970.

name: Nicholas Riddell
description: A Roman Catholic priest (Fr. Nick Riddell, age 39, the oldest of the group), he was one of the fifteen who burned Chicago draft records on May 25, 1969. He was indicted on the four federal counts and was among the ten convicted in June 1970; sentences for the group ran up to two years.

case.charges: Destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy (the May 25, 1969 Chicago draft-record burning).
case.convicted: Most were convicted in June 1970.

name: Margaret Katroscik
description: A Catholic laywoman (age 22), Katroscik was one of the fifteen who broke into the Chicago Selective Service office and burned roughly 40,000 draft records on May 25, 1969. She was indicted on the four federal counts. She was among those tried in 1970 (10 of 11 tried were convicted).

case.charges: Destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy (the May 25, 1969 Chicago draft-record burning).
case.convicted: Most were convicted in June 1970.

name: Linda Quint
description: A laywoman (age 22), Quint was one of the fifteen who burned some 40,000 Chicago draft records on May 25, 1969. She was indicted on the four federal counts (destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with Selective Service, and conspiracy). Group sentences ran up to two years.

case.charges: Destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy (the May 25, 1969 Chicago draft-record burning).

name: Fred Chase
description: One of the fifteen (age 25) who broke into the Chicago Selective Service office at 2355 W. 63rd Street and burned roughly 40,000 draft records on May 25, 1969, waiting at the scene to be arrested. He was indicted on the four federal counts; ten of the eleven tried were convicted in June 1970, with sentences up to two years.

case.charges: Destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy (the May 25, 1969 Chicago draft-record burning).

name: Les Bayless
description: A young layperson (age 22) living at the 'Blair House' commune near the draft board, Les Bayless was one of three men who on May 21, 1969 walked into the Silver Spring, Maryland Selective Service office and destroyed several hundred draft records with blood and black paint, then waited for the FBI. Already out on bail for draft resistance, he received a 5-year sentence for draft evasion plus an additional 3-year sentence (from Judge Roszel C. Thomsen) for the draft-board action. He was later interviewed for the 2013 documentary 'Hit & Stay.'

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the May 21, 1969 Silver Spring, MD draft-board raid).
case.convicted: Convicted.

name: Jon Bayless
description: A layperson and, at age 17, the youngest of the Silver Spring Three, Jon Bayless (brother of Les Bayless) took part in the May 21, 1969 destruction of several hundred draft records at the Silver Spring, Maryland Selective Service office, mutilating files with blood and paint and ransacking the office before waiting to be arrested. He was charged for his participation in the draft-board action; his specific sentence was not found.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the May 21, 1969 Silver Spring, MD draft-board raid).
case.convicted: Convicted.

name: Michael Bransome
description: A layperson (age 18) living at the Blair House commune, Bransome was one of the three who destroyed several hundred draft records at the Silver Spring, Maryland Selective Service office on May 21, 1969. He was sentenced to 3 years in federal prison, served about 8 months, and after receiving a death threat from inmates fled to Canada in 1970 and was granted political asylum in Sweden in 1971.

case.charges: Destruction of Selective Service records (the May 21, 1969 Silver Spring, MD draft-board raid).
case.convicted: Convicted.

name: Marc Edelman
description: A cabinetmaker who was one of five men who publicly burned their draft cards at Union Square, New York City, on November 6, 1965. He was convicted for the act; the resulting appeal, United States v. Edelman (2d Cir. 1967), bears his name, and he was sentenced to six months in prison.

case.charges: Destruction of a Selective Service registration certificate (the November 6, 1965 Union Square, NYC draft-card burning).
case.convicted: Three of the five (Cornell, Edelman, Lisker) were convicted — United States v. Edelman — and sentenced to six months.

name: Roy Lisker
description: Writer, mathematician, and self-described Renaissance man who was one of five men who burned their draft cards at Union Square on November 6, 1965, at a rally organized by the Committee for Non-Violent Action. Though he said he was not himself draft-eligible, he burned a card as a statement against the war; he was convicted alongside Cornell and Edelman and sentenced to six months.

case.charges: Destruction of a Selective Service registration certificate (the November 6, 1965 Union Square, NYC draft-card burning).
case.convicted: Three of the five (Cornell, Edelman, Lisker) were convicted — United States v. Edelman — and sentenced to six months.

name: David Paul O'Brien
description: On March 31, 1966, David Paul O'Brien and three companions burned their draft cards on the steps of the South Boston Courthouse before a crowd that included FBI agents; the crowd then attacked the burners. Prosecuted under the 1965 amendment, he was convicted and sentenced to the maximum six years as a youth offender under the Youth Corrections Act. His appeal produced the landmark Supreme Court decision United States v. O'Brien (1968), which held that draft-card burning was not protected symbolic speech.

case.charges: Destruction of a Selective Service registration certificate (the March 31, 1966 South Boston Courthouse draft-card burning), 18 U.S.C. 462(b).
case.convicted: Convicted.
case.sentence: Sentenced to the maximum six years under the Youth Corrections Act; his appeal produced the landmark Supreme Court decision United States v. O'Brien (1968).

name: Barry Bondhus
description: In February 1966, 19-year-old Barry Bondhus of Big Lake, Minnesota, dumped two buckets of human feces (collected by him and his eleven brothers) into the 1-A files at the Elk River draft board, in what became known as 'the Big Lake One' and is often cited as the first draft-board raid of the movement. He was convicted of destroying government property and interfering with the Selective Service and served about 14 months in federal prison.

case.charges: Destruction of government property and interfering with the Selective Service System (the February 1966 Elk River, MN draft-board raid, 'the Big Lake One').
case.convicted: Convicted.
case.sentence: Served about 14 months in federal prison.

name: Bruce Dancis
description: On December 14, 1966, 18-year-old Cornell University SDS activist Bruce Dancis tore his draft card into four pieces before a crowd, then mailed the pieces to the Selective Service. His act helped inspire the April 1967 Central Park 'burn-in.' He was indicted and convicted of draft-card mutilation and served about 19 months in federal prison, entering in May 1969; he later wrote the memoir 'Resister.'

case.charges: Mutilation of a Selective Service registration certificate (tore up his draft card at Cornell, December 14, 1966).
case.convicted: Convicted.
case.sentence: Served about 19 months in federal prison, entering in May 1969.

name: Gary Rader
description: A former Army Special Forces (Green Beret) reservist who, wearing his uniform, burned his draft card at the April 15, 1967 Spring Mobilization 'burn-in' in the Sheep Meadow of Central Park, New York City. He was arrested by FBI agents days later at his home in Evanston, Illinois, and was reportedly the only person charged with a federal crime out of that rally. He later helped found the Chicago Area Draft Resisters (CADRE).

case.charges: Destruction or mutilation of a Selective Service registration certificate (draft card) under the 1965 federal law.
case.convicted: Convicted.

name: Stephen L. Smith
description: A University of Iowa student who burned his draft card on October 20, 1965, at the Iowa Memorial Union in Iowa City, one of the earliest prosecutions under the 1965 law. He was convicted in November 1966 and sentenced to three years' probation.

case.charges: Destruction or mutilation of a Selective Service registration certificate (draft card) under the 1965 federal law.
case.convicted: Convicted.
